content: To improve the collection and use of administrative data on violence against women (VAW), it is essential to establish a robust system that includes training and resource allocation. In Uganda, mapping the administrative data environment for VAW and harmonizing data collection processes are critical steps. Analyzing the willingness of relevant data producers to participate will determine whether it is feasible to collect data from all service providers within or across sectors or whether the system should initially focus on specialized VAW service providers. Specialized VAW services have certain advantages. Personnel in these services are trained in VAW and have a clear mandate, which motivates data collection and use. Additionally, these services represent a smaller group of data producers, simplifying the implementation of the administrative data system. However, focusing solely on specialized services limits the scope of data collection, as it excludes survivors who do not access these services. For instance, many countries have specialized family and domestic violence units within their police and justice systems, but these units often have limited coverage and interact with only a small portion of VAW survivors. Many survivors report violence to general police officers, and their cases are handled by prosecutors outside specialized units. Similarly, health systems may have specialized sexual assault services, but collecting data only from these services overlooks survivors who seek care from non-specialized services. Survivors may access healthcare due to VAW-related injuries or be identified as experiencing VAW during visits to departments like obstetrics, gynecology, or emergency care. General services have the potential to collect data from a broader range of survivors, but the quality of data may suffer without adequate training and dedicated resources. Furthermore, the large volume of other information collected in general services may limit the amount of VAW data recorded, emphasizing the need for a parsimonious approach. Focusing exclusively on specialized services further narrows the already limited representation of survivors in VAW administrative data. While expanding data collection to general services may seem challenging, training to improve understanding and response to VAW in these settings represents an opportunity to enhance services for survivors. Even if general services initially record few cases, initiating data collection can make VAW more visible and, over time, improve both data quality and service delivery. Ideally, VAW administrative data should be collected from both general services and specialized VAW services. Whether this approach is immediately feasible or requires a phased implementation—starting with specialized services and expanding to general services—depends on the legal, policy, and data environment. This decision should be made by the coordination mechanism after a thorough review. Producers of VAW administrative data include organizations and institutions that document services provided to prevent and address VAW in the health, justice, and social services sectors. These may include public, non-governmental, or private sector organizations, as well as ministries, departments, national statistics offices, and international organizations. Data users, on the other hand, come from a wide range of institutions, including policymakers, service managers, academics, researchers, media, civil society organizations, and the private sector. Many institutions serve as both data producers and users. Institutionalized dialogue between data producers and users can strengthen trust, improve data quality, and align data production with user needs. In the context of developing or improving a VAW administrative data system, broad consultations with current and potential data users and producers can inform the minimum data set and support planning for data use and communication. Such dialogues do not guarantee that all desired information will be included in the minimum data set or that the system will meet all expressed needs. However, they provide valuable insights into user priorities and help build relationships between data producers and users. For example, in Jamaica, user-producer dialogues on VAW administrative data were convened in 2021 as part of a collaboration between the Planning Institute of Jamaica and UN Women. This initiative, supported by the EU-UN Spotlight Initiative, aimed to strengthen VAW data production and use. Eleven dialogues were held across all 14 parishes, with one special interest dialogue involving churches. These virtual meetings, necessitated by COVID-19 restrictions, brought together representatives from various sectors to discuss their experiences providing services to VAW survivors, the data needed, and the data currently produced. The dialogues revealed valuable information about service delivery and data collection processes, such as the different points at which survivors might interact with services and the information currently collected. Understanding these contexts is crucial for designing data collection methodologies and a minimum data set that aligns with service workflows. The dialogues also highlighted the extent of VAW data collection, resource and capacity development needs, and the importance of clear protocols and ethical guidelines for data sharing. The findings from these dialogues, along with an analysis of data collection and statistical capacities, informed the development of a proposed minimum data set. This set includes variables such as the number, age, and gender of survivors and perpetrators, the survivor-perpetrator relationship, types of VAW experienced, services provided, and outcomes of protection order applications and police reports. Collecting this data is critical for designing comprehensive policies and programs for VAW prevention and response. To ensure effective data collection, institutional capacity development should focus on implementing the agreed minimum data set. This includes documenting all types of VAW reported by survivors and creating a complete picture of the violence experienced. Collecting data on the survivor-perpetrator relationship, as well as their sex and age, provides insights into power dynamics and helps monitor service demand and response quality. Additional variables, such as gender identity, sexual orientation, disability status, ethnicity, and citizenship, may also be collected based on national and subnational priorities. Ultimately, a comprehensive VAW administrative data system can identify strengths and gaps in sectoral and cross-sectoral responses, contributing to more effective prevention and response efforts at the national and subnational levels.
